title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: when, where and how many

questions.prompt: A guide claims that distance study lets the learner work whenever and wherever he chooses. A pupil replies: you are wrong, it takes as much time as a classroom course. Why does that reply contradict nothing?

options.text: flexibility and a time commitment are two names for one thing
only a learner who had followed both kinds could say it
the claim answers when and where; the reply counts hours
the claim counted hours; the reply answers when and where

questions.explanation: Contradiction needs two statements about the same thing, and these two are not about the same thing. The guide says who picks the hour of the work and the room it happens in; the pupil says how much of the week it eats. A learner can hold every one of his hours by his own choosing and still owe the course as many as a classroom would have taken, so both remarks stand together untouched. Swapping which statement carried which question leaves exactly the same failure, only backwards. Treating a freedom and a quantity as one thing is worse still: it would make any demanding course automatically a free one. And having followed both kinds of programme is not what this reply lacks — a reply that met the claim would do its work whoever had written it.

questions.prompt: Tick EVERY line in which a phrase explaining the noun in front of it is fenced by a comma at each end.

options.text: Salwa Gharbi, a nurse on night duty, studies between two shifts.
The review, a quarterly published in Tunis, printed three replies.
Sami Trabelsi, the youngest learner on the course gave up television.
The course an eight-month programme in three languages, opens in October.
The pupils wrote to the author, the magazine and their teacher.

questions.explanation: Two lines are fenced at both ends and go to press as they stand: the phrase saying what Salwa Gharbi is sits between two commas immediately after her name, and the phrase saying what sort of publication the review is does the same work for it. In each case the explanation can be lifted out and a whole sentence remains. The line about Sami Trabelsi opens its fence and never closes it, so the reader is told an explanation has begun and left to guess where it ends; the line about the course does the opposite, closing a fence that was never opened, which is why the words run into one another in front of the comma. The line about the pupils is correctly punctuated and still fails the instruction: its commas are keeping the items of a list apart, which is the comma's other job on this page and not the one being checked.

questions.prompt: A pupil quotes one of the three e-learners in his letter. Which sentence claims no more than a quotation can support?

options.text: It is now proved that an online course costs more time than a classroom one.
A magazine checked it before printing, so it may be taken as fact.
Nothing can be said about the hours; all we have are opinions.
An e-learner wrote in 2003 that his course was as heavy as a classroom one.

questions.explanation: A quotation is a witness, and a witness reports a belief. Name the man, date the words and say what he found: that much a quotation will carry, and it leaves the reader free to weigh it. Turn the same remark into a proof and you have claimed what no quotation can give you — that the thing itself is so, because somebody wrote it down. A magazine prints what its readers send it, and printing is not checking; a sentence that says otherwise invents an authority nobody ever exercised. The opposite fault costs just as much: refuse the remark even as evidence of what one learner found, and you are left with nothing at all to argue from, in a letter that was asked for arguments.

questions.prompt: Told that somebody short of time can make more of it, a learner replies that a day holds twenty-four hours and no more. What has he misread?

options.text: making time moves hours from one use to another; it adds none
making time does lengthen the day, which he has just denied
making time means finding a course that asks fewer hours of him
making time means counting up the hours a week already holds

questions.explanation: He is right about the day and wrong about the phrase. Nobody was proposing to stretch anything: to make time is to find hours that are already committed and commit them elsewhere, which is exactly what the printed example does when it takes them out of sleep. Read the phrase as an addition of hours, as he has, and the objection becomes unanswerable — and that is the sign that the reading is wrong, since the remark was made by somebody who also knew how long a day is. Nor is it a hunt for a lighter course: the demand is the demand, and the whole point is that it can be met without one extra hour in the day. Counting the hours a week already holds would tell him the size of his problem and move not one of them.

questions.prompt: A pupil has granted that a distance learner picks his own hour and place. He must counter that claim without withdrawing the grant and without giving offence. Which sentence does it?

options.text: Anybody who values that freedom has never sat down to a course.
The freedom is real, and it lets a course go unopened for a term.
The freedom is not real, since the course must end by a fixed date.
The freedom is real enough, and I can put nothing beside it.

questions.explanation: The strong move keeps the concession and turns it: the freedom stands, and the very thing that makes it valuable is shown to carry a cost. Nothing has been taken back and nobody has been insulted, yet the claim no longer stands alone. Denying that the freedom is real cancels the grant outright and reopens an argument the pupil had already settled in the other man's favour — a closing date says when the work must be finished, not when it may be done. Granting the point and confessing there is nothing to set beside it is polite and is no counter at all. And an insult answers a person instead of a claim, which is the one thing the instruction rules out.

questions.prompt: A learner writes that online study, like all learning, wants hours. Delete the three fenced words, says a classmate, since the sentence works without them. What would it lose?

options.text: the claim that time is all that learning has ever demanded
nothing: the words repeat what the rest of the line already says
the claim that this kind of learning is not the exception
the claim that this kind of learning is the heavier one

questions.explanation: The classmate is right about the grammar and wrong about the sentence. Fence the three words out and what remains is a complete statement — that is what makes them an addition. But they were carrying the argument: by putting this kind of learning beside every other kind, they refuse it any special case, which is the answer to a reader who came to the page believing that a course followed at home is a lighter thing. They claim no extra burden, only an equal one, so reading them as a complaint about a heavier load says something the sentence never said. They say nothing about time being all that learning wants, either — attention, patience and a place to work go unmentioned rather than denied. And repetition is the one thing they are not: nothing else in the line mentions any other kind of learning at all.
